key_insights: Freshman-year course choices matter as much as or more than the grades received, because they function as prerequisites that shape the rest of a student's available course sequence (e.g., honors physics freshman year enabling AP Physics senior year).

Colleges are described as more forgiving of weak freshman-year grades than of weak grades in upper-level coursework, since sophomore/junior/senior performance is seen as more predictive of college readiness.

States that University of California schools exclude both freshman and senior year grades from the GPA calculation they use in admissions, calculating GPA from summer after freshman year through summer after junior year.
A rising grade trend (weak start, strong finish) is described as viewed more favorably by admissions committees than a declining trend (strong start, weak finish).
Cites Yale as an example of a school that considers a counselor's letter explaining a rough freshman year more valuable than a note in the Common App's optional 'additional information' section.
Advises against overcorrecting a weak freshman year by joining many activities later, which can look scattered; recommends roughly 2-6 meaningful, sustained extracurriculars instead.
Notes that non-traditional commitments (part-time jobs, family/caregiving responsibilities, medical issues) can and should be included in the activities section, not just conventional clubs/sports.
